metadata.scope: e_yongliang (all baronies across k_guannei, k_hexi, and k_xia)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_xinping.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) records that in Sui Kaihuang 4 (584 CE), Baitu County (白土縣) was renamed Xinping County (新平縣) after Xinping Commandery (established 194 CE in Eastern Han).
b_xinping.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 新平 (Xīnpíng, 'new and pacified/level'), originally an auspicious commandery name created in 194 CE (Eastern Han) and applied to the county seat (modern Binzhou, Shaanxi) in 584 CE.

historical_names.name: Baitu
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上); Book of Wei (魏書·地形志)
historical_names.notes: Known as Baitu County (白土縣) under Northern Wei and Western Wei before being renamed Xinping in 584 CE.

b_sanshui.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) record Sanshui County (三水縣) as established in Western Wei (535–557 CE) in modern Xunyi County, Shaanxi.
b_sanshui.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 三水 (Sānshuǐ, 'three waters'), named for the three converging springs/streams in the local Luo River valley (羅川谷三泉並流).

historical_names.name: Xunyi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Originally established as Xunyi County (栒邑縣) in Qin/Western Han before Western Wei renamed it Sanshui.

b_yilu.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) notes Yilu County (宜祿縣) was merged into Chungu under Northern Zhou, and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records it was re-established in 628 CE (Zhenguan 2) using the abolished Northern Wei (386–534 CE) county name.
b_yilu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 宜祿 (Yílù, 'fitting emolument/blessing'), an auspicious administrative name first used in Northern Wei and revived in 628 CE under Tang Binzhou (modern Changwu County, Shaanxi).

b_fangqu.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records Fangqu County (方渠縣) was established in Tang Jinglong 1 (707 CE) by splitting Maling County under Qingzhou (modern Huanxian, Gansu).
b_fangqu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 方渠 (Fāngqú, 'square canal'), named after an irrigation canal at the Tang frontier garrison in Qingzhou (later Huanzhou).

b_luoyuan.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) records Luoyuan County (洛源縣) was established in Sui Daye 1 (605 CE) under Honghua Commandery (modern Wuqi County, Shaanxi).
b_luoyuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 洛源 (Luòyuán, 'source of the Luo River'), a locator compound referring to the headwaters of the Beiluo River (北洛河).

b_huaian_2.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records Huaian County (懷安縣) was established in Tang Kaiyuan 10 (722 CE) in Qingzhou to resettle fugitive households.
b_huaian_2.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 懷安 (Huái'ān, 'cherish and pacify'), an auspicious Tang administrative name reflecting frontier pacification and resettlement.

b_dingan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 490 CE (Northern Wei Taihe 14) as Ding'an County (定安縣), seat of Binzhou (邠州) and later Ningzhou (寧州) in modern Ningxian, Gansu.
b_dingan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 定安 (Dìng'ān, 'stabilized peace'), an auspicious administrative name for the seat of Ningzhou.

b_pengyuan.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) records that in Sui Kaihuang 18 (598 CE), Pengyang County (彭陽縣) was renamed Pengyuan County (彭原縣).
b_pengyuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 彭原 (Péngyuán, 'Peng plateau'), adapted from the earlier Northern Wei name Pengyang (彭陽) in modern Qingyang/Ningxian, Gansu.

historical_names.name: Pengyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Known as Pengyang County (彭陽縣) under Northern Wei before Sui Kaihuang 18 (598 CE).

b_xiangle.first_mention_attestation: Established in Northern Wei Taihe 11 (487 CE) as Xiangle County (襄樂縣), seat of Xiangle Commandery (modern Xiangle Town, Ningxian, Gansu).
b_xiangle.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 襄樂 (Xiānglè, 'assisting joy/harmony'), an auspicious Northern Wei administrative name.

b_anhua.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records that in Tang Shenlong 1 (705 CE), the seat of Qingzhou was renamed Anhua County (安化縣) (modern Qingcheng County, Gansu).
b_anhua.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 安化 (Ānhuà, 'pacifying and civilizing'), a Tang imperial-ideological county name.

historical_names.name: Heshui
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上); Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Originally established in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) as Heshui/Honghua before being renamed Anhua in 705 CE.

historical_names.name: Honghua
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上); Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Originally established in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) as Heshui/Honghua before being renamed Anhua in 705 CE.

b_tongchuan.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records that in Tang Wude 3 (620 CE), Sanquan County was moved to Tongchuan Citadel and renamed Tongchuan County (同川縣).
b_tongchuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 同川 (Tóngchuān, 'united valley/streams'), named after Tongchuan Citadel (同川城) in Tang Qingzhou.

historical_names.name: Sanquan
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Established in Sui Yining 2 (618 CE) as Sanquan County before being renamed Tongchuan in 620 CE.

b_huachi.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Tang records attest Huachi County (華池縣) as re-established in Sui Renshou 2 (602 CE) (and earlier in Western Wei) in modern Huachi County, Gansu.
b_huachi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 華池 (Huáchí, 'splendid pool'), named after the ancient Huachi Water (華池水, modern Erjiangchuan River) in Gansu.

b_tianxing.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records Tianxing County (天興縣) was created in Tang Zhide 2 (757 CE) by splitting Yong County (雍縣) as the metropolitan county of Fengxiang Prefecture.
b_tianxing.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 天興 (Tiānxīng, 'heaven-prospering'), an auspicious Tang dynastic name commemorating Emperor Suzong's temporary western capital at Fengxiang.

historical_names.name: Yong
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志上); Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Originally Yong County (雍縣) from Qin/Han times; merged into Tianxing in Baoying 1 (762 CE).

b_purun.first_mention_attestation: Established in Sui Daye 1 (605 CE) from the Purun military colony (普潤屯) and attested in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) under Fengxiang Prefecture (modern Linyou County, Shaanxi).
b_purun.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 普潤 (Pǔrùn, 'universally enriching/irrigating'), named after the Sui-era Purun agricultural colony (普潤屯).

b_mei.first_mention_attestation: Established as Mei County (郿縣) upon Qin's unification in 221 BCE (after the Spring and Autumn settlement Meiyi 郿邑) and attested in Book of Han (漢書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一).
b_mei.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 郿 (Méi), an ancient Qin settlement name derived from local terrain shaped like an eyebrow (眉) along the Wei River (modern Meixian, Shaanxi).

b_qianyuan.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) records that in Sui Kaihuang 5 (585 CE), Qianyin County was renamed Qianyuan County (汧源縣), seat of Longzhou (modern Longxian, Shaanxi).
b_qianyuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 汧源 (Qiānyuán, 'source of the Qian River'), a locator compound referring to the headwaters of the Qian River (汧水).

historical_names.name: Qianyin
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Established in Western Wei (535–557 CE) as Qianyin County, briefly renamed Duyang, and renamed Qianyuan in 585 CE.

historical_names.name: Duyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Established in Western Wei (535–557 CE) as Qianyin County, briefly renamed Duyang, and renamed Qianyuan in 585 CE.

b_qianyang.first_mention_attestation: Established in Northern Wei Zhengguang 3 (522 CE) as Qianyang County (汧陽縣) under Qianyang Commandery and attested in Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一).
b_qianyang.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 汧陽 (Qiānyáng, 'north/sunny side of the Qian River'), a locator compound (modern Qianyang County, Shaanxi).

b_wushan.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records that in Tang Zhenguan 1 (627 CE), Changshe County (長蛇縣) was renamed Wushan County (吳山縣) under Longzhou.
b_wushan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 吳山 (Wúshān, 'Mount Wu'), named after the sacred western peak Mount Wuyue (吳岳 / 吳山) in Baoji, Shaanxi.

historical_names.name: Changshe
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上); Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Previously Changshe County (長蛇縣) in Sui before being renamed Wushan in 627 CE.

b_yichuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in Western Wei Datong 3 (537 CE) as Yichuan County (義川縣) and attested in Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) as seat of Danzhou (modern Yichuan County, Shaanxi).
b_yichuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 義川 (Yìchuān, 'righteous valley/stream'), a Western Wei auspicious administrative name.

b_yunyan.first_mention_attestation: Taiping Huanyu Ji (太平寰宇記·卷35) records that in Western Wei Datong 13 (547 CE), Yongping County was renamed Yunyan County (雲岩縣); also attested in Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一).
b_yunyan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 雲岩 (Yúnyán, 'cloud crag'), named after Mount Yunyan (雲岩山) in Danzhou (modern Yichuan County, Shaanxi).

historical_names.name: Yongping
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyu Ji (太平寰宇記·卷35)
historical_names.notes: Previously Yongping County (永平縣) in Western Wei before being renamed Yunyan in 547 CE.

b_zhongbu.first_mention_attestation: Established by Later Qin in Hongshi 1 (399 CE) as Zhongbu County (中部縣), seat of Zhongbu Commandery, and attested in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) under Fangzhou (modern Huangling County, Shaanxi).
b_zhongbu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 中部 (Zhōngbù, 'central division'), a directional/administrative name from Later Qin (briefly Neibu 內部 under Sui to avoid a naming taboo).

b_shengping.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records Shengping County (昇平縣 / 升平縣) was established in Tang Tianbao 12 (753 CE) by splitting Yijun County under Fangzhou.
b_shengping.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 昇平 / 升平 (Shēngpíng, 'ascending peace/prosperity'), an auspicious Tang era/county name.

b_chengcheng.first_mention_attestation: Established in Northern Wei Taiping Zhenjun 7 (446 CE) as Chengcheng County (澄城縣), seat of Chengcheng Commandery, and attested in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) under Tongzhou.
b_chengcheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 澄城 (Chéngchéng), historically a Northern Wei orthographic alteration of Zheng (徵 / 北徵) due to homophony, combined with 城 ('walled city').

historical_names.name: Zheng
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Originally Beizheng (北徵) in Qin and Zheng County (徵縣) in Western Han before Northern Wei established Chengcheng in 446 CE.

historical_names.name: Beizheng
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Originally Beizheng (北徵) in Qin and Zheng County (徵縣) in Western Han before Northern Wei established Chengcheng in 446 CE.

b_luojiao.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) records Luojiao County (洛交縣) was established in Sui Kaihuang 3 (583 CE; some sources cite 596 CE) as seat of Fuzhou (modern Fuxian, Shaanxi).
b_luojiao.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 洛交 (Luòjiāo, 'confluence of the Luo River'), a locator compound referring to the junction of the Beiluo River and its tributaries.

b_luochuan.first_mention_attestation: Established under Later Qin (384–417 CE) as Luochuan County (洛川縣) and attested in Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) under Fuzhou.
b_luochuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 洛川 (Luòchuān, 'Luo River'), named after the Beiluo River flowing through the county in Shaanxi.

b_zhiluo.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records Zhiluo County (直羅縣) was established in Tang Wude 3 (620 CE) at Zhiluo Citadel under Fuzhou (modern Zhiluo Town, Fuxian, Shaanxi).
b_zhiluo.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 直羅 (Zhíluó), explained in Old Book of Tang as 'the citadel overlooks the Luo River (羅水), whose valley is level and straight (其川平直)'.

b_fushi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fushi County (膚施縣) in Warring States Wei/Qin (c. 358 BCE), attested in Book of Han (漢書·地理志上) under Shang Commandery and in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) as seat of Yanzhou (modern Yan'an, Shaanxi).
b_fushi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 膚施 (Fūshī), an ancient Warring States toponym of Shang Commandery (later re-established in Sui Daye 3, 607 CE, at modern Yan'an).

b_fuzheng.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一) records that in Tang Tianbao 1 (742 CE), Jincheng County (金城縣) was renamed Fuzheng County (敷政縣) under Yanzhou.
b_fuzheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 敷政 (Fūzhèng, 'promulgate governance'), a Tang Tianbao-era auspicious administrative renaming.

historical_names.name: Yincheng
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上); Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Originally Yincheng County (因城縣) in Northern Wei, moved and renamed Jincheng County (金城縣) in Tang Wude 2 (619 CE), then renamed Fuzheng in 742 CE.

historical_names.name: Jincheng
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上); Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一)
historical_names.notes: Originally Yincheng County (因城縣) in Northern Wei, moved and renamed Jincheng County (金城縣) in Tang Wude 2 (619 CE), then renamed Fuzheng in 742 CE.

b_jinming.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) lists Jinming County (金明縣) under Yan'an Commandery (607 CE), renamed from Northern Wei Guangluo County (modern Ansai District, Yan'an, Shaanxi).
b_jinming.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 金明 (Jīnmíng, 'golden brightness'), a Sui-era county name replacing Northern Wei Guangluo (廣洛).

historical_names.name: Guangluo
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志一); Wikipedia (安塞区)
historical_names.notes: Established as Guangluo County (廣洛縣) in Northern Wei before being renamed Jinming under Sui.

b_yanchuan.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) records that in Sui Kaihuang 3 (583 CE), Wen'an County was renamed Yanchuan County (延川縣) after the Tuyan River (吐延川) (modern Yanchuan County, Shaanxi).
b_yanchuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 延川 (Yánchuān), abbreviated from the hydronym Tuyanchuan / Tuyan River (吐延川 / 吐延水, modern Qingjian River).

historical_names.name: Wen'an
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Established in Western Wei (535–557 CE) as Wen'an County (文安縣) before being renamed Yanchuan in 583 CE.

b_baoan.first_mention_attestation: Not attested in 867 CE; Bao'an Military Prefecture (保安軍) was established in Northern Song (977 CE, Taiping Xingguo 2) on the site of Tang Kaolaocheng / Shencejun, and elevated to Bao'an County by Jin in 1172 CE (modern Zhidan County, Shaanxi).
b_baoan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 保安 (Bǎo'ān, 'protect and pacify'), a Song frontier military prefecture name (977 CE) post-dating the 867 CE baseline.

historical_names.name: Kaolaocheng
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyu Ji (太平寰宇記); Da Qing Yitongzhi (大清一統志)
historical_names.notes: In Tang Xianheng (670–674 CE) and Zhenyuan 14 (798 CE), the site was known as Kaolaocheng (拷栳城) and Shencejun (神策軍) before becoming Bao'an in Song.

historical_names.name: Shencejun
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyu Ji (太平寰宇記); Da Qing Yitongzhi (大清一統志)
historical_names.notes: In Tang Xianheng (670–674 CE) and Zhenyuan 14 (798 CE), the site was known as Kaolaocheng (拷栳城) and Shencejun (神策軍) before becoming Bao'an in Song.

b_xicheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Book of Han (漢書·地理志上) as Xicheng County (西城縣) under Hanzhong Commandery (established in Qin/Western Han), and in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志二) as seat of Jinzhou (modern Ankang, Shaanxi).
b_xicheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 西城 (Xīchéng, 'western walled city'), a directional compound from Qin/Han times.

b_ankang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Western Jin Taikang 1 (280 CE) when Anyang County was renamed Ankang County (安康縣) (later renamed Hanyin in 757 CE; Jinzhou itself was also styled Ankang Commandery in 742–757 CE).
b_ankang.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 安康 (Ānkāng, 'peaceful and prosperous').

historical_names.name: Anyang
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志二)
historical_names.notes: Originally Han Anyang County (安陽縣, c. 198 BCE) before Western Jin renamed it Ankang in 280 CE.

b_shiquan.first_mention_attestation: Established in Western Wei Feidi 1 (552 CE) when Yongle County was renamed Shiquan County (石泉縣), attested in Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志二).
b_shiquan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 石泉 (Shíquán, 'stone springs'), named for the numerous springs emerging from rock crevices south of the town (城南石隙多泉).

historical_names.name: Anle
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Established under Southern Qi (479–502 CE) as Anle County and renamed Yongle under Liang before Western Wei renamed it Shiquan in 552 CE.

historical_names.name: Yongle
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (隋書·地理志上)
historical_names.notes: Established under Southern Qi (479–502 CE) as Anle County and renamed Yongle under Liang before Western Wei renamed it Shiquan in 552 CE.

b_xunyang_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Book of Han (漢書·地理志上) as Xunyang County (旬陽 / 洵陽) under Hanzhong Commandery, and in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志二) under Jinzhou (modern Xunyang, Shaanxi).
b_xunyang_2.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 洵陽 / 旬陽 (Xúnyáng, 'north/sunny side of the Xun River'), a locator compound in southern Shaanxi.

b_shangluo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise) as Shangluo County (上雒县) under Hongnong Commandery, established by the early Western Han (c. 202 BCE; later written 上洛县 and made seat of Shangluo Commandery in 266 CE under Western Jin).
b_shangluo.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 上 (shàng, 'upper') + 洛 (Luò, 'Luo River'), referring to the settlement's location on the upper reaches of the Luo River (South Luo River) in southeastern Shaanxi.

b_shangjin.first_mention_attestation: Documented as Shangjin County (上津县), seat of Shangjin Commandery established by the Southern Liang dynasty before its capture by Western Wei in 552 CE (Book of Sui, Geographical Treatise).
b_shangjin.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 上 (shàng, 'upper') + 津 (jīn, 'ford, ferry crossing'), denoting an upper river crossing on the Jiahe/Han River borderlands between Shaanxi and Hubei.

b_shanglo.first_mention_attestation: In 584 CE (Kaihuang 4 of the Sui dynasty), Shang County (商县) was renamed Shangluo County (商洛县) under Shangzhou (Old Book of Tang / Book of Sui).
b_shanglo.etymology_analysis: Compound of 商 (Shāng, from Mount Shang and the ancient Shang fief/county) and 洛 (Luò, from the Luo River), adopted in 584 CE to reflect the region's two defining geographic names.

historical_names.name: Shang
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) / Book of Han (Hanshu)
historical_names.notes: Previously Shang County (商县), established under the Qin dynasty (221 BCE) and named after Mount Shang and Shang Yang's fief.

historical_names.name: Shang County
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) / Book of Han (Hanshu)
historical_names.notes: Previously Shang County (商县), established under the Qin dynasty (221 BCE) and named after Mount Shang and Shang Yang's fief.

b_qianyuan_1.first_mention_attestation: In 758 CE (Qianyuan 1 of Emperor Suzong of Tang), Anye County (安业县) was renamed Qianyuan County (乾元县) after the imperial era name (Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang).
b_qianyuan_1.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tang dynasty era name Qianyuan (乾元, 758–760 CE) of Emperor Suzong, itself derived from the Book of Changes (Yijing) phrase '乾元' (primal creative power of Heaven).

historical_names.name: Anye
historical_names.source: New Book of Tang (Geographical Treatise) / Dushi Fangyu Jiyao
historical_names.notes: Originally established in 696 CE (Wansui Tongtian 1) as Anye County (安业县) before being renamed Qianyuan in 758 CE.

b_tonggu.first_mention_attestation: Established by Western Wei (c. 553 CE) when Baishi County (白石县) was renamed Tonggu County (同谷县), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_tonggu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 同 (tóng, 'united/common') + 谷 (gǔ, 'valley'), referring to the Tonggu valley basin in southeastern Gansu.

historical_names.name: Baishi
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu, Geographical Treatise)
historical_names.notes: Known as Baishi County (白石县) prior to the Western Wei renaming to Tonggu.

b_shanglu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise) as Shanglu County (上禄县) under Wudu Commandery, established in 111 BCE (Yuanding 6 of Emperor Wu of Han).
b_shanglu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 上 (shàng, 'upper/high') + 禄 (lù, 'emolument/blessing'), an auspicious Han-era county name in Wudu Commandery (southern Gansu).

b_changdao.first_mention_attestation: In 598 CE (Kaihuang 18 of the Sui dynasty), Shuinan/Hanyang County was renamed Changdao County (长道县), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_changdao.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 长 (cháng, 'long') + 道 (dào, 'road/frontier district'), reflecting the long mountain corridor through southern Gansu.

historical_names.name: Shuinan
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu) / Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties
historical_names.notes: Established under Northern Wei as Shuinan County (水南县) and Hanyang Commandery before being renamed Changdao in 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Hanyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu) / Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties
historical_names.notes: Established under Northern Wei as Shuinan County (水南县) and Hanyang Commandery before being renamed Changdao in 598 CE.

b_jiangli.first_mention_attestation: Renamed from Anyu County (安育县) to Jiangli County (将利县) under Emperor Xiaomin of Northern Zhou (557 CE), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_jiangli.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 将 (jiàng, 'general') + 利 (lì, 'advantage/benefit'), an auspicious military-administrative name bestowed by the Northern Zhou dynasty.

historical_names.name: Shimen
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu, Geographical Treatise)
historical_names.notes: Originally Northern Wei Shimen County (石门县), renamed Anyu County (安育县) by Western Wei, then Jiangli County (将利县) by Northern Zhou.

historical_names.name: Anyu
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu, Geographical Treatise)
historical_names.notes: Originally Northern Wei Shimen County (石门县), renamed Anyu County (安育县) by Western Wei, then Jiangli County (将利县) by Northern Zhou.

b_fujin.first_mention_attestation: In 892 CE (Jingfu 1 of Emperor Zhaozong of Tang), Fujin County (覆津县) was renamed Fujin County (福津县) with the auspicious character 福 ('blessing'), documented in the New Book of Tang (卷四十 地理四).
b_fujin.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 福 (fú, 'blessing/fortune') + 津 (jīn, 'ferry ford'), an auspicious 892 CE Tang-era respelling of the earlier 覆津 (Fùjīn) adopted alongside the renaming of Wuzhou to Jiezhou.

historical_names.name: Fujin
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu) / New Book of Tang
historical_names.notes: Established under Western Wei as Fujin County (覆津县), which remained the official name in 867 CE until being renamed 福津 in 892 CE.

b_hezheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hezheng County (和政县) under Northern Zhou (557–581 CE) alongside Taocheng Commandery, documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_hezheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 和 (hé, 'harmony') + 政 (zhèng, 'governance'), an auspicious political-administrative name coined during the Northern Zhou dynasty.

b_youchuan.first_mention_attestation: In 712 CE (Xiantian 1 of Tang), Jicheng County (基城县) was renamed Youchuan County (祐川县) to observe the naming taboo of Emperor Xuanzong (Li Longji).
b_youchuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 祐 (yòu, 'divine protection/blessing') + 川 (chuān, 'river/stream valley'), coined in 712 CE to replace 基城 (Jīchéng) due to the imperial taboo on the character 基.

historical_names.name: Jicheng
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu) / Tang Huiyao
historical_names.notes: Originally Jicheng County (基城县) under Northern Zhou (by 561 CE), renamed Youchuan in 712 CE due to Emperor Xuanzong's personal name taboo.

b_huaidao.first_mention_attestation: Established under Northern Zhou (c. 566 CE, Tianhe 1, when Dangzhou was created) as Huaidao County (怀道县), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_huaidao.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 怀 (huái, 'cherish/pacify') + 道 (dào, 'the Way / frontier district'), reflecting Northern Zhou pacification policy in the Dangchang Qiang borderlands.

b_chengji.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chengji County (成纪县) by the Qin state/dynasty (by 221 BCE) in Longxi Commandery, attested in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) and Book of Han (Hanshu).
b_chengji.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 成 (chéng, 'accomplish') + 纪 (jì, 'order/annals'), an ancient Qin-era county name in eastern Gansu.

b_qingshui.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise) as Qingshui County (清水县) under Tianshui Commandery, established in 114 BCE (Yuanding 3 of Emperor Wu of Han).
b_qingshui.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 清 (qīng, 'clear') + 水 (shuǐ, 'water/river'), named after the clear Qingshui River flowing through the county.

b_shanggui.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise) as Shanggui County (上邽县) in Longxi Commandery, prefixed with 上 ('upper') to distinguish it from Xiagui (下邽) in Guanzhong.
b_shanggui.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 上 (shàng, 'upper') + 邽 (Guī, from the Gui Rong people conquered by Qin in 688 BCE), distinguishing the upper Longxi settlement from Xiagui in Shaanxi.

historical_names.name: Gui
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin)
historical_names.notes: Originally established as Gui County (邽县) in 688 BCE (Duke Wu of Qin year 10) after conquering the Gui Rong.

b_longcheng_2.first_mention_attestation: Documented as Longcheng County (陇城县) under Lueyang Commandery during the Former Qin and Later Qin dynasties (4th century CE), and restored in 586 CE (Sui Kaihuang 6).
b_longcheng_2.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 陇 (Lǒng, Mount Long / Longshan) + 城 (chéng, 'walled city/fortress'), denoting the fortified town at the foot of Mount Long.

b_longxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Longxi Commandery (陇西郡) by the State of Qin during the Warring States period (c. 279 BCE, King Zhaoxiang of Qin), attested in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) and Book of Han (Hanshu).
b_longxi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 陇 (Lǒng, Mount Long / Longshan) + 西 (xī, 'west'), a directional compound meaning 'west of Mount Long'.

b_weiyuan.first_mention_attestation: In 551 CE (Datong 17 of Western Wei), Shouyang County (首阳县) was renamed Weiyuan County (渭源县), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_weiyuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 渭 (Wèi, 'Wei River') + 源 (yuán, 'source/headwaters'), a locator compound referring to the headwaters of the Wei River at Niaoshu Mountain.

historical_names.name: Shouyang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Biography of Feng Fengshi)
historical_names.notes: Originally Shouyang County (首阳县) in the Han dynasty (attested 42 BCE) before being renamed Weiyuan in 551 CE.

b_liangquan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Liangquan County (梁泉县) under Cao Wei (220–265 CE) and later seat of Gudao Commandery and Nanqi/Fengzhou under Northern Wei (526 CE), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_liangquan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 梁 (liáng, 'bridge/ridge') + 泉 (quán, 'spring'), derived from the earlier Liangquan garrison (梁泉戍) in southwestern Shaanxi.

b_hechi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise) as Hechi County (河池县) under Wudu Commandery, established in 111 BCE (later temporarily Guanghua under Northern Wei and restored to Hechi in 601 CE).
b_hechi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 河 (hé, 'river') + 池 (chí, 'pool'), named after the Hechi River/pool (河池水) in southeastern Gansu.

b_shunzheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shunzheng Commandery (顺政郡) under Western Wei (c. 553 CE) and renamed Shunzheng County (顺政县) in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_shunzheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 顺 (shùn, 'obedient/compliant') + 政 (zhèng, 'governance'), an auspicious administrative name bestowed after Western Wei conquered the region.

historical_names.name: Ju
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Book of Sui (Suishu)
historical_names.notes: Originally Ju County (沮县) in the Han dynasty, later Wuxing (武兴) and Hanqu (汉曲) under Western Wei before becoming Shunzheng.

historical_names.name: Wuxing
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Book of Sui (Suishu)
historical_names.notes: Originally Ju County (沮县) in the Han dynasty, later Wuxing (武兴) and Hanqu (汉曲) under Western Wei before becoming Shunzheng.

historical_names.name: Hanqu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Book of Sui (Suishu)
historical_names.notes: Originally Ju County (沮县) in the Han dynasty, later Wuxing (武兴) and Hanqu (汉曲) under Western Wei before becoming Shunzheng.

b_changju.first_mention_attestation: Established as Changju County (长举县) under Western Wei (c. 553 CE) alongside Pantou Commandery, documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_changju.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 长 (cháng, 'long/enduring') + 举 (jǔ, 'raise/elevate'), a Western Wei administrative county name in Xingzhou (modern Lueyang, Shaanxi).

b_zheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zheng County (郑县) in 687 BCE (Duke Wu of Qin year 11: '初县杜、郑'), attested in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin).
b_zheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 郑 (Zhèng), named after the original Western Zhou fief of the State of Zheng (established by Duke Huan of Zheng in 806 BCE) before its eastward migration.

b_huayin.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Huayin County (华阴县) under Emperor Gaozu of Han (c. 199 BCE, Book of Han, Geographical Treatise), from earlier Ningqin County.
b_huayin.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 华 (Huà, 'Mount Hua') + 阴 (yīn, 'north/shady side of a mountain'), a directional locator compound meaning 'north of Mount Hua'.

historical_names.name: Yinjin
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) / Book of Han (Hanshu)
historical_names.notes: Known as Yinjin (阴晋) under the State of Wei during the Warring States period, renamed Ningqin (宁秦) by Qin, and Huayin by Han.

historical_names.name: Ningqin
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) / Book of Han (Hanshu)
historical_names.notes: Known as Yinjin (阴晋) under the State of Wei during the Warring States period, renamed Ningqin (宁秦) by Qin, and Huayin by Han.

b_xiagui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xiagui County (下邽县) in 688 BCE (Duke Wu of Qin year 10), attested in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin) and Zizhi Tongjian.
b_xiagui.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 下 (xià, 'lower') + 邽 (Guī, the Gui Rong people resettled here from Longxi), distinguishing it from Shanggui ('Upper Gui') in Gansu.

b_changan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chang'an County (长安县) in 202 BCE (Emperor Gaozu of Han year 5), attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise).
b_changan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 长 (cháng, 'perpetual') + 安 (ān, 'peace/stability'), meaning 'Perpetual Peace', taken from the Qin-era Chang'an Township (长安乡).

b_jingyang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 352 CE under the Former Qin dynasty by partitioning Chiyang County to create Jingyang County (泾阳县) in Xianyang Commandery.
b_jingyang.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 泾 (Jīng, 'Jing River') + 阳 (yáng, 'north/sunny bank of a river'), a directional locator compound meaning 'north of the Jing River'.

b_lantian.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lantian County (蓝田县) in 379 BCE (Duke Xian of Qin year 6), attested in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) and Book of Han (Hanshu).
b_lantian.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 蓝 (lán, 'indigo/blue-green jade') + 田 (tián, 'field'), named after Mount Lantian (famous for its jade deposits) in southeastern Guanzhong.

b_zhouzhi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhouzhi County (盩厔县) in 104 BCE (Taichu 1 of Emperor Wu of Han) under Youfufeng, attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise).
b_zhouzhi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 盩 (zhōu, 'mountain bend') + 厔 (zhì, 'river bend'), describing the terrain where the Qinling Mountains curve and the Wei River bends.

b_liquan.first_mention_attestation: In 598 CE (Kaihuang 18 of the Sui dynasty), Ningyi County (宁夷县) was renamed Liquan County (醴泉县) after the local sweet spring, documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_liquan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 醴 (lǐ, 'sweet wine') + 泉 (quán, 'spring'), named after a local spring whose water was described as tasting like sweet wine.

historical_names.name: Gukou
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Book of Sui (Suishu)
historical_names.notes: Han-era Gukou County (谷口县) and Northern Wei Ningyi County (宁夷县) preceded the 598 CE renaming to Liquan.

historical_names.name: Ningyi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Book of Sui (Suishu)
historical_names.notes: Han-era Gukou County (谷口县) and Northern Wei Ningyi County (宁夷县) preceded the 598 CE renaming to Liquan.

b_pingyi.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 104 BCE (Taichu 1 of Emperor Wu of Han) as Zuo Pingyi (左冯翊), one of the Three Guardians (Sanfu) of the Han capital region (Book of Han, Geographical Treatise); later Pingyi County in 607 CE.
b_pingyi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 冯 (píng, 'support/rely on') + 翊 (yì, 'assist/flank'), an official title meaning 'supporting and assisting the capital' (Chang'an) that became the regional and county name.

b_heyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Heyang County (郃阳县) in 155 BCE (Emperor Jing of Han year 2) by changing 合 to 郃, attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise).
b_heyang_1.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 郃 (Hé, 'He River') + 阳 (yáng, 'north/sunny bank of a river'), a directional locator compound meaning 'north of the He River'.

historical_names.name: Heyangyi
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) / Book of Han (Hanshu)
historical_names.notes: Originally established in 330 BCE (King Huiwen of Qin year 8) as Heyangyi (合阳邑) before the Han-era orthography 郃阳 in 155 BCE.

b_fucheng.first_mention_attestation: In early Daye (c. 605–607 CE) of the Sui dynasty, Fucheng County (敷城县) was respelled Fucheng County (鄜城县), documented in the Book of Sui (卷二十九 地理上).
b_fucheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 鄜 (Fū, from the Fushui River and Fuzhou) + 城 (chéng, 'walled city'), a Sui-era orthographic modification of the Northern Wei name 敷城.

b_huayuan.first_mention_attestation: In 586 CE (Kaihuang 6 of the Sui dynasty), Niyang County (泥阳县) was renamed Huayuan County (华原县) as seat of Yizhou, documented in the Book of Sui and Old Book of Tang.
b_huayuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 华 (huá, 'splendid') + 原 (yuán, 'high plateau/plain'), referring to the loess plateau north of the Wei River valley in central Shaanxi.

historical_names.name: Niyang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise)
historical_names.notes: Previously Niyang County (泥阳县), established in the Western Han dynasty, before being renamed Huayuan in 586 CE.

b_fuping.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geographical Treatise) as Fuping County (富平县) under Beidi Commandery (c. 114 BCE; later relocated to Guanzhong in Shaanxi during the Jin/Northern Wei period).
b_fuping.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 富 (fù, 'wealthy/abundant') + 平 (píng, 'peaceful/level'), an auspicious Han-era county name meaning 'abundant and peaceful'.

b_yunyang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 350 BCE (12th year of Duke Xiao of Qin) as Yunyang County (云阳县) in Guannei, Shaanxi; continuously attested through the Han and Tang dynasties (Xin Tangshu Vol. 37).
b_yunyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym meaning 'sunny south slope of the cloud-shrouded mountain' (referring to Mount Yun / Mount Ganquan in Shaanxi). Founded as a Qin county in 350 BCE.

b_zhangye.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (Yuanding 6th year, Western Han) as Zhangye Commandery (张掖郡) in the Hexi Corridor; attested in Shiji, Hanshu, and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE).
b_zhangye.etymology_analysis: Chinese imperial strategic name meaning 'extending the arm' (from the Han phrase '张国臂掖，以通西域', extending the empire's arm to reach the Western Regions).

b_shandan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (Western Han) as Shandan County (删丹县) under Zhangye Commandery; attested in Hanshu Geography Treatise and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE).
b_shandan.etymology_analysis: Chinese rendering of the Xiongnu/local name associated with Mount Shandan (焉支山), later also written 山丹 (Shandan).

b_yanzhi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 121 BCE during Huo Qubing's Hexi campaign in Shiji (匈奴列传: '过焉支山千余里') and later in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE).
b_yanzhi.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription of a Xiongnu oronym (Mount Yanzhi), famously associated with safflower dye ('rouge') and Xiongnu songs lamenting its loss.

b_jiankang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiankang Commandery (建康郡) in Hexi under Former Liang (4th century CE) and re-established in 695 CE (Wu Zhou Zhengsheng 1st year) as Jiankang Army (建康军) by Wang Xiaojie, attested in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE) and Xin Tangshu Vol. 40.
b_jiankang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese military/administrative name meaning 'establish peace and prosperity'.

b_qilian.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 121 BCE in Shiji and Hanshu ('祁连山') following Huo Qubing's Hexi campaign, and as Tang Qilian Post (祁连戍) in Xin Tangshu Vol. 40.
b_qilian.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription of a Xiongnu word meaning 'heaven/sky' (hence 'Heavenly Mountains'), applied to the Qilian Mountain range.

b_jiuquan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 121 BCE (populated 111 BCE) by the Western Han as Jiuquan Commandery (酒泉郡), one of the Four Commanderies of Hexi; attested in Shiji, Hanshu, and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE).
b_jiuquan.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym meaning 'Wine Spring', named after a spring beneath the city wall whose water tasted like wine (or from legend of Huo Qubing pouring imperial wine into the spring).

b_dongting.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 813 CE in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40 (and Xin Tangshu Vol. 40) as Mount Dongting (洞庭山), 70 li west of Jiuquan County in Suzhou.
b_dongting.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'Cavern Hall Mountain', attested in Tang geographical treatises for a gold-bearing mountain west of Jiuquan.

b_fulu.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fulu County (福禄县) in 295 CE (Western Jin Yuankang 5th year) from Han Lufu County, and re-established in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) under Suzhou (Xin Tangshu Vol. 40).
b_fulu.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese county name meaning 'blessing and prosperity', an inversion of its Western Han name Lufu (禄福).

historical_names.name: Lufu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Lufu County (禄福县) in Jiuquan Commandery; Western Jin inverted the characters to Fulu (福禄) in 295 CE.

b_liaoquan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Liaoquan Garrison-City (蓼泉守捉城), a High Tang frontier garrison 120 li west of Ganzhou prior to the Tibetan conquest of Ganzhou in 766 CE, recorded in Xin Tangshu Vol. 40.
b_liaoquan.etymology_analysis: Chinese topographic toponym meaning 'Smartweed Spring', referring to an oasis spring west of Zhangye/Ganzhou.

b_ganjun.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 554 CE (Western Wei Feidi 3rd year) as the namesake of Ganzhou ('因州东甘峻山为名') and explicitly described in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE) as Mount Ganjun (甘峻山).
b_ganjun.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'Sweet and Lofty Mountain', located northeast of Zhangye and famous in Tang sources for its falcons.

b_heli.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Heli Mountain (合黎山) in the pre-Qin/Han Shangshu (Yugong: '导弱水，至于合黎'), Hanshu, Shuijingzhu, and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE).
b_heli.etymology_analysis: Ancient Chinese oronym (also called Yaotu Mountain in Tang sources) along the northern edge of the Zhangye–Gaotai corridor.

b_yumen.first_mention_attestation: Established c. 111–102 BCE (Western Han) as Yumen Pass (玉门关, Jade Gate Pass) and later Yumen County (玉门县); continuously attested in Hanshu, Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE), and Xin Tangshu Vol. 40.
b_yumen.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym meaning 'Jade Gate', named for the Khotanese jade caravans entering China through the western frontier pass.

b_jinshan.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 813 CE in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40 under Yumen County, Suzhou: '金山，在县东六十里。出金' (Mount Jinshan, 60 li east of Yumen, producing gold).
b_jinshan.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'Gold Mountain', a gold-bearing mountain east of Tang Yumen County.

b_dudeng.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 813 CE in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40 (and Xin Tangshu Vol. 40) under Yumen County, Suzhou: '独登山，在县北十里。其山出盐' (Mount Dudeng, 10 li north of Yumen, producing tribute salt).
b_dudeng.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'Solitary Ascent Mountain', a salt-producing mountain north of Tang Yumen County.

b_zhenwu.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Hexi/Liangzhou in 994 CE (Northern Song Chunhua 5th year) in Songshi Vol. 492 ('振武军都罗族大首领' alongside Xiliangfu/Six Valleys Tibetans); distinct from the 745 CE Tang Zhenwu Army in Shuofang (Inner Mongolia).
b_zhenwu.etymology_analysis: Chinese military garrison name meaning 'Rousing Martial Valor', attested in the Liangzhou/Hexi region in the late 10th century (post-867 CE).

b_baiting.first_mention_attestation: Established in 751 CE (Tang Tianbao 10th year, or 755 CE per Xin Tangshu) as Baiting Army (白亭军), upgraded from Baiting Garrison (白亭守捉) by Geshu Han, 300 li north of Liangzhou (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40).
b_baiting.etymology_analysis: Chinese frontier garrison name meaning 'White Post', named after Baiting Lake (白亭海) and an adjacent white watch-post north of Liangzhou.

b_jinchang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 295 CE (Western Jin Yuankang 5th year) as Jinchang Commandery (晋昌郡), and renamed Jinchang County (晋昌县) in 621 CE (Tang Wude 4th year) as the seat of Guazhou (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40).
b_jinchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese administrative name meaning 'Prosperity of the Jin', coined when Western Jin created Jinchang Commandery in 295 CE.

historical_names.name: Ming'an
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Ming'an County (冥安县) in Dunhuang Commandery; Western Jin made it the seat of Jinchang Commandery in 295 CE, and Tang renamed it Jinchang County in 621 CE.

b_changle.first_mention_attestation: Established under Northern Wei (Emperor Xiaoming, c. 524 CE) as Changle Commandery (常乐郡), later Sui Changle Town (常乐镇) and Tang Changle County (常乐县, 622 CE) in Guazhou (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40).
b_changle.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese administrative name meaning 'Eternal Joy', replacing earlier Han Guangzhi / Cao Wei Yihe.

historical_names.name: Guangzhi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally Western Han Guangzhi County (广至县) and Cao Wei Yihe County (宜禾县) before Northern Wei established Changle Commandery.

historical_names.name: Yihe
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally Western Han Guangzhi County (广至县) and Cao Wei Yihe County (宜禾县) before Northern Wei established Changle Commandery.

b_yonggui.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Yonggui Garrison (雍归镇 / 壅归镇) in 10th-century Cao-era Guiyijun Dunhuang manuscripts (e.g., P.4640 Guiyijun Poli, c. 924 CE) as one of the Eight Garrisons of Guiyijun; no pre-867 CE written attestation found.
b_yonggui.etymology_analysis: Chinese garrison name meaning 'Harmonious Allegiance', referring to the fortified stone settlement at modern Shibaocheng in Subei/Guazhou.

b_hehe.first_mention_attestation: Established in 705 CE (Tang Shenlong 1st year) as Hehe Post (合河戍), 80 li northeast of Jinchang County in Guazhou (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40), also called Hehe Garrison (合河镇) in Xin Tangshu Vol. 40.
b_hehe.etymology_analysis: Chinese topographic name meaning 'Confluence of Rivers', a Tang garrison northeast of Guazhou.

b_baizhang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Baizhang Garrison (百帐守捉), a Tang military post 120 li beyond Hehe Garrison in Guazhou prior to the Tibetan conquest of Guazhou in 776 CE, recorded in Xin Tangshu Vol. 40.
b_baizhang.etymology_analysis: Chinese military/frontier name meaning 'Hundred Tents', referring to a Tang outpost near nomadic encampments northeast of Guazhou.

b_xinghu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as 'Xinghu' (兴湖, 'Prospering Lake') in historical sources <= 867 CE; appears to be an in-game or modern homophonic alteration of the Tang lake Xinghubo (兴胡泊, 'Lake where Hu merchants gather') attested in Shazhou Dudufu Tujing (c. 700 CE).
b_xinghu.etymology_analysis: Chinese compound 'Prospering Lake', unattested in Hexi/Guasha before 867 CE; likely derived from or confused with the Tang-era lake Xinghubo (兴胡泊) in Shazhou.

b_dunhuang_2.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (Western Han Yuanding 6th year) as Dunhuang Commandery (敦煌郡) and Dunhuang County; continuously attested in Shiji, Hanshu, and Tang sources.
b_dunhuang_2.etymology_analysis: Chinese imperial name glossed in Tang sources as 'great and flourishing' (敦，大也; 煌，盛也), or a Han transcription of an older local/Yuezhi ethnonym.

b_mogao.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 698 CE (Wu Zhou Shengli 1st year) on the Li Jun Mogao Caves Buddhist Niche Stele (李君莫高窟佛龛碑) in Cave 332, referring to the Mogao administrative district (莫高乡) and cave complex.
b_mogao.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Tang administrative district (莫高乡) at the Mogao Caves southeast of Dunhuang, meaning 'high/lofty' (or reflecting a local/steppe substrate).

b_shouchang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 619 CE (Tang Wude 2nd year) as Shouchang County (寿昌县) in Shazhou, named after Shouchang Marsh (寿昌泽) to its south (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40; Xin Tangshu Vol. 40).
b_shouchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese county name meaning 'Longevity and Prosperity', taken from the nearby Shouchang Marsh.

historical_names.name: Longle
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang Shouchang County was established in 619 CE on the seat of the Western Han Longle County (龙勒县).

b_yangguan.first_mention_attestation: Established under Western Han Emperor Wu (c. 111–102 BCE) as Yangguan (阳关, Yang Pass) south of Yumen Pass; attested in Hanshu, Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE), and Tang poetry.
b_yangguan.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym meaning 'South Pass' (so named because it lay south of Yumen Pass, guarding the southern Silk Road route from Dunhuang).

b_longle.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (Western Han) as Longle County (龙勒县) in Dunhuang Commandery, named after Mount Longle (Hanshu; Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40).
b_longle.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym named after Mount Longle ('Dragon Bridle'), an ancient Han county southwest of Dunhuang.

b_xincheng.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 900 CE (Tang Guanghua 3rd year / Guiyijun) as Xincheng Garrison (新城镇) in Shazhou in Zhang Baoshan's eulogy (张保山邈真赞); no pre-867 CE written attestation found.
b_xincheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym meaning 'New Fortress/City', one of the Eight Garrisons of the Guiyijun in Shazhou attested from 900 CE onward.

b_mingshui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mingshui (冥水, Ming River) in Shuijingzhu (6th century CE) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40 (813 CE: '本汉冥安县... 因县界冥水为名也'), the namesake of Han Ming'an County.
b_mingshui.etymology_analysis: Chinese hydronym meaning 'Dark River', flowing from the Tuyuhun/Qilian border into the marshlands of Guazhou (ancient Shule River system).

b_ziting.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 701 CE (Wu Zhou Dazu 1st year) in Dunhuang manuscript S.3669 (大足元年沙州敦煌县效谷乡户籍: '沙州子亭镇将'), referring to Ziting Garrison in Shazhou.
b_ziting.etymology_analysis: Chinese frontier garrison name meaning 'Subordinate/Small Post', attested in Tang Dunhuang household registers from 701 CE.

b_ganquan.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 700 CE in the Tang Dunhuang manuscript Shazhou Tujing / Shazhou Dudufu Tujing (P.2005 & S.2593) as Ganquan Water (甘泉水), feeding the irrigation canals south and southwest of Shazhou.
b_ganquan.etymology_analysis: Chinese hydronym meaning 'Sweet Spring', attested in Tang Dunhuang geographical manuscripts as the primary water source for Shazhou's canals.

b_baishan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 73 CE (Hou Hanshu) as Mount Baishan (白山, eastern Tian Shan), and in Hexi proper as Baishan Post (白山戍), 150 li northeast of Changsong County in Liangzhou (Xin Tangshu Vol. 40).
b_baishan.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'White Mountain' (snow-capped peak), applied to the Tang Baishan Post in Liangzhou and to the eastern Tian Shan.

b_xinquan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 701 CE (Wu Zhou Dazu 1st year) by Guo Yuanzhen as Xinquan Army (新泉军) 200 li northwest of Huizhou on the eastern Hexi frontier (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40; Xin Tangshu Vol. 37).
b_xinquan.etymology_analysis: Chinese military garrison name meaning 'New Spring', founded in 701 CE by Tang general Guo Yuanzhen on the Hexi–Huizhou frontier.

b_fanhe.first_mention_attestation: Established under Western Han as Fanhe County (番禾县) in Zhangye Commandery, later Fanhe Commandery under Northern Liang, and renamed Tianbao County in 744 CE (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi Vol. 40).
b_fanhe.etymology_analysis: Ancient Chinese county name (pronounced Pánhé in Han/Tang glosses, '番音盘') in the Liangzhou–Yongchang corridor, attested since Western Han.

b_xiutu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 121 BCE (Shiji and Hanshu) as the territory of the Xiongnu Xiutu King (休屠王) in the Hexi Corridor; Western Han subsequently established Xiutu County (休屠縣) under Wuwei Commandery.

morphemes.translation: First syllable of Xiongnu tribal/royal title Xiutu
Second syllable of Xiongnu tribal/royal title Xiutu

b_xiutu.etymology_analysis: Phonetic transcription of the Xiongnu title Xiutu (休屠), whose bearer ruled the Wuwei area until defeated by Huo Qubing in 121 BCE.

b_guangwu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 326 CE (Former Liang Jianxing 14th year) as Guangwu County (廣武縣) within Guangwu Commandery, as recorded in Jinshu and Zizhi Tongjian.
b_guangwu.etymology_analysis: Auspicious military-frontier name ('Vast Martiality') given to the Former Liang county and commandery in modern Yongdeng, Gansu.

b_yunjie.first_mention_attestation: Established in 60 BCE (Han Xuan-di Shenjue 2nd year) as Yunjie County (允街縣) under Jincheng Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28b, Geography Treatise).

morphemes.translation: First element of Yunjie (read Yán per Meng Kang's Hanshu commentary)

b_yunjie.etymology_analysis: Western Han county in Jincheng Commandery (允街, modern Yongdeng/Honggu area, Gansu).

b_herong.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 701 CE (Wu Zhou Dazu 1st year): Tang commander Guo Yuanzhen (郭元振) built Herong Fortress (和戎城) at Xiaokou on Liangzhou's southern border simultaneously with Baiting Army, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 122, Biography of Guo Yuanzhen), Zizhi Tongjian (Vol. 207), and Da Tang Xinyu (Vol. 4).
b_herong.etymology_analysis: Frontier garrison name meaning 'Pacifying the Rong' (和戎), built as Herong Fortress (和戎城) at Xiaokou on Liangzhou's southern border by Tang commander Guo Yuanzhen in 701 CE.

b_guzang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Guzang County (姑臧縣) under Wuwei Commandery in Western Han (c. 101 BCE), attested in Hanshu (Vol. 28b) on the site of an earlier Xiongnu fortress (Gaizang).

morphemes.translation: First syllable of Xiongnu toponym Guzang (variant of Gaizang 蓋臧)
Second syllable of Xiongnu toponym Guzang

b_guzang.etymology_analysis: Sinicized transcription of a Xiongnu settlement name (姑臧, also written Gaizang 蓋臧), later the capital of Liangzhou and the Five Liang states.

b_changsong.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Changsong (昌松) under Later Liang (386–392 CE, Changsong Commandery and County), continuing Western Han Cangsong County (倉松縣, 101 BCE) in Wuwei Commandery.
b_changsong.etymology_analysis: Auspicious orthographic variant of Western Han Cangsong (倉松, 'Granary Pine'), adopted in the Sixteen Kingdoms period (Later Liang) and retained in Sui and Tang.

historical_names.name: Cangsong
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Book of Han), Vol. 28b
historical_names.notes: Originally established in Western Han Wuwei Commandery (c. 101 BCE) as Cangsong County (倉松縣) before being written Changsong (昌松) under Later Liang.

b_shenwu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 620 CE (Tang Wude 3rd year) as Shenwu County (神烏縣), serving as seat of Liangzhou, recorded in Jiu Tangshu and Xin Tangshu.
b_shenwu.etymology_analysis: Tang-dynasty county in Liangzhou (modern Wuwei, Gansu), literally 'Divine Raven', briefly renamed Wuwei County (695–705 CE) before reverting to Shenwu.

b_zhanyin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zhanyin County (鸇陰縣) in 111 CE (Eastern Han Yongchu 5th year) when transferred from Anding Commandery to Wuwei Commandery, recorded in Hou Hanshu (Treatise on Commanderies and States).

morphemes.translation: Sparrowhawk or falcon (variant of 鶉 chún)
Shady north slope or south bank of a river

b_zhanyin.etymology_analysis: Directional/topographic locator compound ('Falcon-Yin', south bank of the Yellow River crossing in modern Jingyuan/Pingchuan, Gansu), succeeding Western Han Chunyin (鶉陰).

historical_names.name: Chunyin
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Book of Han), Vol. 28b
historical_names.notes: Attested in Western Han Anding Commandery (114 BCE) as Chunyin (鶉陰), later written Zhanyin (鸇陰) in Eastern Han (111 CE).

b_aowei.first_mention_attestation: Established in Western Han (c. 101 BCE) as Aowei County (媼圍縣) under Wuwei Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28b, Geography Treatise).
b_aowei.etymology_analysis: Western Han county in Wuwei Commandery (modern Jingtai County, Gansu), retained through Eastern Han and Cao Wei before being abolished under Western Qin.

b_zhiyang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 81 BCE (Han Zhaodi Shiyuan 6th year) as Zhiyang County (枝陽縣) under Jincheng Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28b, Geography Treatise).

morphemes.translation: Sunny south slope or north bank of a river

b_zhiyang.etymology_analysis: Directional/topographic locator compound ('Sunny side of the river branch'), a Western Han county in Jincheng Commandery (modern Yongdeng, Gansu).

b_fuhan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 81 BCE among the initial counties of Western Han Jincheng Commandery (Hanshu Vol. 28b; local tradition also attributes its founding to the Qin dynasty after subduing the Hanqiang).
b_fuhan.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement in modern Linxia, Gansu, associated with the Hanqiang (罕羌) tribe; later seat of Hezhou (河州) and Fuhan Commandery.

b_daxia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 8 BCE (Han Chengdi Suihe 1st year) as Daxia County (大夏縣) under Longxi Commandery in Hanshu (Vol. 28b, Geography Treatise).
b_daxia.etymology_analysis: Western Han county in Longxi Commandery (大夏, modern Guanghe/Linxia, Gansu).

b_kangle.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1073 CE (Northern Song Xining 6th year) when Wang Shao built Kangle City (康樂城), renamed Kangle Zhai (康樂寨) in the same year.
b_kangle.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Song-dynasty fortress name (康乐, 1073 CE) in modern Linxia, Gansu.

b_guangwei.first_mention_attestation: Established under the Northern Wei dynasty (386–534 CE) as Guangwei County (廣威縣) under Taohe Commandery (modern Hualong/Jianzha, Qinghai), later seat of Kuozhou / Ninghai Commandery in Tang.
b_guangwei.etymology_analysis: Auspicious frontier county name ('Vast Prestige') established under Northern Wei in eastern Qinghai and retained under Tang Kuozhou.

b_michuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 631 CE (Tang Zhenguan 5th year) as Michuan County (米川縣), recorded in Jiu Tangshu and Xin Tangshu.
b_michuan.etymology_analysis: Tang-dynasty county ('Grain Valley') in eastern Qinghai / upper Yellow River valley (modern Minhe/Jishishan area).

b_jincheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 81 BCE (Han Zhaodi Shiyuan 6th year) as Jincheng County (金城縣), initial seat of Jincheng Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Vol. 28b).
b_jincheng_1.etymology_analysis: Western Han frontier citadel ('Metal/Golden Citadel', denoting impregnability per Chen Zan's Hanshu commentary), predecessor of Lanzhou.

b_didao.first_mention_attestation: Established by the Qin dynasty (by 221 BCE) as Didao County (狄道縣), long-time seat of Longxi Commandery, attested in Shiji and Hanshu (Vol. 28b).
b_didao.etymology_analysis: Qin-Han administrative march ('Di March') in modern Lintao, Gansu; per Hanshu, counties with non-Han populations were designated 'dao' (道).

b_huangshui.first_mention_attestation: Established in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18th year) when Xidu County was renamed Huangshui County (湟水縣), seat of Shanzhou (modern Ledu, Qinghai), named after the Huangshui River.
b_huangshui.etymology_analysis: Sui- and Tang-dynasty county seat of Shanzhou (modern Ledu, Qinghai), named directly after the Huangshui River (attested since Han times).

historical_names.name: Poqiang
historical_names.source: Ledu District Wikipedia / Hanshu (Vol. 28b)
historical_names.notes: Established as Poqiang County (破羌縣) in 60 BCE, later Xidu County (西都縣), and renamed Huangshui County in 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Xidu
historical_names.source: Ledu District Wikipedia / Hanshu (Vol. 28b)
historical_names.notes: Established as Poqiang County (破羌縣) in 60 BCE, later Xidu County (西都縣), and renamed Huangshui County in 598 CE.

b_longzhi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 554 CE (Western Wei Gongdi 1st year) when Doulu Yong'en was enfeoffed as Marquis of Longzhi County (龍支縣侯), recorded in Zhoushu and funerary epitaphs.
b_longzhi.etymology_analysis: Western Wei county in Shanzhou (modern Minhe/Ledu area, Qinghai), renamed from Jincheng County at Longzhi City and retained under Sui and Tang.

b_miaochuan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1023–1024 CE (Northern Song Tiansheng 1st–2nd year) as Miaochuan (邈川), a seat of the Gusiluo (Tsongkha) Tibetan confederation, recorded in Songshi (Vol. 492).
b_miaochuan.etymology_analysis: Song-era Chinese name ('Remote Valley') for the Ledu valley seat of the Tibetan Gusiluo state (11th century CE), later renamed Huangzhou and Lezhou.

historical_names.name: Huangshui
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Suishu, 598 CE; earlier Poqiang audited on b_huangshui)
historical_names.notes: Modern Ledu was Huangshui County (598 CE; earlier Poqiang, audited on b_huangshui) before being called Miaochuan in the 11th century CE.

b_gemen.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for a settlement named Gemen (閤門) in Qinghai; however, Shuijingzhu (He Shui) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao record Gemen River (閤門河) as the classical alternate name for the Haomen River (浩亹河, modern Datong River) joining the Huangshui near Xining/Ledu ('湟水又東與閤門河合，即浩亹河也').
b_gemen.etymology_analysis: From the classical hydronym Gemen River (閤門河, alternate reading/name of the Haomen / Datong River in Shuijingzhu), referring to the river's gate-like canyon; no settlement of this name is attested <= 867 CE.

b_qilin.first_mention_attestation: Qilian County (祁連縣, rendered Qilin here) was first established as Qilian Preparatory Bureau in 1938 CE (ROC 27th year) and became Qilian County in 1953 CE; not an ancient settlement, though named after the ancient Qilian Mountains.

morphemes.translation: First syllable of Xiongnu oronym Qilian ('Heaven')
Second syllable of Xiongnu oronym Qilian

b_qilin.etymology_analysis: Modern Qinghai county (1938/1953 CE) named after the Qilian Mountains (from Xiongnu *qilian* 'heaven'); per audit rules, the ancient mountain name is not conflated with the modern county.

b_semnyi.first_mention_attestation: Xianmi (仙米, Semnyi) is attested as a Qing-era Gelug monastery (Xianmi Temple 仙米寺) and as an administrative unit from 1952 CE (Xianmi Tibetan Autonomous Region in Menyuan, Qinghai); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.

morphemes.translation: Immortal, transcendent (phonetic rendering of Tibetan Sem-/Seng-)

b_semnyi.etymology_analysis: Chinese phonetic transcription (仙米 Xianmi) of Tibetan Semnyi in Menyuan County, Qinghai, associated with the Qing-era Xianmi Monastery and the 1952 CE township.

b_yalong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical records <= 867 CE; no historical settlement or county named Yalong (亞龍) is documented in the Qilian region of Qinghai.
b_yalong.etymology_analysis: Unattested in-game barony in d_qilian ('Secondary Dragon'), without pre-867 CE historical documentation.

b_yeniugou.first_mention_attestation: Modern PRC-era township (野牛溝鄉) in Qilian County, Qinghai, with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_yeniugou.etymology_analysis: Modern township in Qilian County, Qinghai, named after the Wild Yak Gorge (野牛溝) at the headwaters of the Heihe River.

b_baoding.first_mention_attestation: Established in 756 CE (Tang Zhide 1st year) by renaming Anding County to Baoding County (保定縣) in Jingzhou (modern Jingchuan, Gansu), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 37).
b_baoding.etymology_analysis: Tang-dynasty auspicious renaming ('Preserve Stability') of Han-era Anding County during the An Lushan Rebellion (756 CE).

historical_names.name: Anding
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Book of Han) / Anding Commandery
historical_names.notes: Originally Anding County (安定縣) in Han Anding Commandery (114 BCE), renamed Baoding County in 756 CE.

b_linjing.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 8 BCE (Han Chengdi Suihe 1st year) as Linjing County (臨涇縣) under Anding Commandery in Hanshu (Vol. 28b, Geography Treatise).
b_linjing.etymology_analysis: Relational/locator compound ('Overlooking the Jing River'), a Western Han county in Anding Commandery (modern Zhenyuan County, Gansu).

b_liangyuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 607 CE (Sui Daye 3rd year) as Liangyuan County (良原縣) under Anding Commandery in Suishu (Geography Treatise) and continued in Tang Jingzhou.
b_liangyuan.etymology_analysis: Sui- and Tang-dynasty county ('Fertile Plateau') in Jingzhou (modern Lingtai County, Gansu).

b_xioaguan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 112 BCE (Han Wudi Yuanding 5th year) when Emperor Wu crossed Xiaoguan (蕭關) into Anding Commandery, recorded in Shiji and Hanshu.
b_xioaguan.etymology_analysis: Ancient strategic pass ('Mugwort Pass') southeast of Guyuan, Ningxia, one of the Four Passes of Guanzhong (spelled 'Xioaguan' in the game file).

b_huaide.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1108 CE (Northern Song Daguan 2nd year) as Huaide Jun (懷德軍) in Guyuan, Ningxia, by elevating Pingxia City (unrelated to the 720 CE Tang honorary title).
b_huaide.etymology_analysis: Northern Song military prefecture ('Cherishing Virtue', 1108 CE) at Huangduobao in Guyuan, Ningxia.

b_pinggao.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 583 CE (Sui Kaihuang 3rd year) as Pinggao County (平高縣), renamed under Western Wei (552–556 CE) from Han-era Gaoping County (modern Guyuan, Ningxia).
b_pinggao.etymology_analysis: Western Wei inversion of Han Gaoping (高平, 'High Plain') to Pinggao (平高), serving as the seat of Yuanzhou in modern Guyuan, Ningxia.

historical_names.name: Gaoping
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Book of Han) / Anding Commandery
historical_names.notes: Originally Gaoping County (高平縣), seat of Western Han Anding Commandery (114 BCE), renamed Pinggao under Western Wei.

b_baiquan.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 607 CE (Sui Daye 3rd year) as Baiquan County (百泉縣) under Pingliang Commandery (Yuanzhou), modern Pengyang County, Ningxia.
b_baiquan.etymology_analysis: Sui- and Tang-dynasty county ('Hundred Springs') in Yuanzhou (modern Pengyang County, Ningxia).

b_pingliang.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 358 CE (Former Qin Yongxing 2nd year) as Pingliang Commandery (平涼郡), followed by Pingliang County (平涼縣) established in 572 CE under Northern Zhou.
b_pingliang.etymology_analysis: Sixteen Kingdoms commandery (358 CE) and Northern Zhou/Tang county ('Pacified/Level Coolness') in eastern Gansu.

b_jinguan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Western Han (c. 102 BCE onward) as Jianshui Jinguan (肩水金關), a fortified pass of the Zhangye Jianshui Command in contemporary Juyan Han bamboo slips.
b_jinguan.etymology_analysis: Western Han frontier checkpoint (Jianshui Jinguan 肩水金關, 'Metal Pass') on the Ruoshui/Heihe corridor in modern Jinta, Gansu.

b_heihe.first_mention_attestation: The Chinese name Heihe (黑河, 'Black River') is a calque of the post-867 CE Tangut designation (𗋽𗰞, 'black water', 11th century CE); in pre-867 CE sources the river was called Ruo Shui (弱水).
b_heihe.etymology_analysis: Hydronym ('Black River') mirroring the 11th-century Tangut name for the Ejin River; earlier Han and pre-Tangut Chinese sources called it Ruo Shui (弱水).

historical_names.name: Ruo Shui
historical_names.source: Shiji / Hanshu and Ejin River Wikipedia
historical_names.notes: In Han-era and pre-Tangut Chinese sources, the river was known as Ruo Shui (弱水, 'Weak Water') before adopting the Tangut-derived name Heihe/Ejin.

b_mazongshan.first_mention_attestation: Republic of China established the Mazongshan Shezhiju (马鬃山设治局) in October 1937 CE in northern Gansu (modern Subei Mongol Autonomous County); Wang Yande's Song-era mention of a 'Mazongshan' refers to a different mountain in Mongolia.
b_mazongshan.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'Horse-Mane Mountain' (马鬃山), descriptive of the mountain ridge's shape in northwestern Gansu. The modern administrative unit began as Mazongshan Shezhiju in 1937 CE.

b_saihantaolai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in modern administrative records of Ejin Banner, Inner Mongolia, where the banner government was stationed at Saihantaolai prior to relocating to Dalaihubu in 1959 CE (now Saihantaolai Sumu).
b_saihantaolai.etymology_analysis: Sinicization of Mongolian Saihan Toorai (ᠰᠠᠢᠬᠠᠨ ᠲᠣᠣᠷᠠᠢ), meaning 'Beautiful Euphrates Poplar', referring to the desert poplar groves in Ejin Banner. The repo calque ('Compete + Han River + Pottery kiln + Arrival') misinterprets the Chinese phonetic characters literally.

b_heicheng.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early 11th century CE (c. 1036–1038 CE) under the Western Xia dynasty as Heishui Zhenyan Military Command (黑水镇燕监军司), later known in Mongolian as Khara-Khoto ('Black City').
b_heicheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese Heicheng ('Black City'), translating Mongolian Khara-Khoto (Qara Qota), and short for Western Xia Heishuicheng ('Black Water City').

historical_names.name: Juyan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) and Juyan Han bamboo slips: Han Juyan Duweifu established in 102 BCE in the surrounding oasis.
historical_names.notes: Western Xia built Khara-Khoto (Heicheng) in the 11th century CE within the ancient Juyan oasis, attested since 102 BCE.

b_sogo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under the name 'Sogo' by 867 CE; Sogo Nuur / Sugu Nuur (索果诺尔/苏古诺尔) is the post-867 CE Mongolian name for East Juyan Lake (东居延海) in Ejin Banner.

morphemes.translation: Mongolian lake name (East Juyan Lake, associated with sogo 'doe')

b_sogo.etymology_analysis: Sinicization of the Mongolian hydronym Sogo Nuur / Sugu Nuur (East Juyan Lake). The repo calque ('Rope bridge + Fruit orchard harvest') misinterprets the Chinese phonetic characters literally.

historical_names.name: Juyan Ze
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu), Book of Jin (Jinshu), and Tang records (Juyan Ze in Han, Juyan Hai since Tang).
historical_names.notes: Sogo Nuur is the eastern basin of ancient Juyan Lake (Juyan Ze / Juyan Hai), attested in Chinese sources from the Han and Tang dynasties.

historical_names.name: Juyan Hai
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu), Book of Jin (Jinshu), and Tang records (Juyan Ze in Han, Juyan Hai since Tang).
historical_names.notes: Sogo Nuur is the eastern basin of ancient Juyan Lake (Juyan Ze / Juyan Hai), attested in Chinese sources from the Han and Tang dynasties.

historical_names.name: Xihai
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu), Book of Jin (Jinshu), and Tang records (Juyan Ze in Han, Juyan Hai since Tang).
historical_names.notes: Sogo Nuur is the eastern basin of ancient Juyan Lake (Juyan Ze / Juyan Hai), attested in Chinese sources from the Han and Tang dynasties.

b_wentugaole.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 20th-century administrative records of Ejin Banner, Inner Mongolia (herders migrated in 1949 CE and returned in 1956 CE; later Wentugaole Commune / Sumu).
b_wentugaole.etymology_analysis: Sinicization of Mongolian Üngtü Gool (ᠦᠩᠲᠦ ᠭᠣᠣᠯ), meaning 'Rich/Beautiful River'. The repo calque misinterprets the Chinese phonetic characters literally.

b_gurinai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in modern administrative records of Ejin Banner, Inner Mongolia, as Gurinai Commune (古日乃公社) in 1981 CE, named after Gurinai / Gurunai Lake (古鲁乃湖).

morphemes.translation: Gurunai (desert lake and oasis name in southeastern Ejin Banner)

b_gurinai.etymology_analysis: Sinicization of Mongolian Gurunai (ᠭᠤᠷᠤᠨᠠᠢ), the name of a desert lake and oasis in southeastern Ejin Banner. The repo calque ('Ancient + Sun + Steppe') misinterprets the Chinese phonetic characters literally.

b_hequ.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tang dynasty records (7th century CE, including the Tang Six Prefectures of Hequ / 河曲六州 established in 679 CE) for the Great Bend of the Yellow River (Hetao).
b_hequ.etymology_analysis: Chinese choronym meaning 'River Bend', the classical and Tang-era designation for the Hetao (Great Bend of the Yellow River) region.

historical_names.name: Henandi
historical_names.source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian): Qin campaign of Meng Tian in 215 BCE.
historical_names.notes: The Ordos/Hetao Yellow River bend region was known as Henandi ('Land South of the River') in Qin-Han sources before the Tang administrative designation Hequ.

b_yuduole.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE, juan 4) recording that during the Tang Tianbao era (742–756 CE), Wang Zhongsi memorialized to establish Jinglue Army at Yuduole City (榆多勒城), northwest of Xiazhou.

morphemes.translation: phonetic element in the Tang fortress name Yuduole

b_yuduole.etymology_analysis: Tang-era frontier fortress name (Yuduolecheng / 榆多勒城) where Jinglue Army (and later Youzhou) was stationed. The repo calque treats the phonetic transcription 多勒 literally.

b_shengwei.first_mention_attestation: Built in Northern Song Tiansheng 2nd year (1024 CE) by Tangut leader Li Deming as Shengwei City (省嵬城) in modern Huinong District, Shizuishan, Ningxia.

morphemes.translation: phonetic element in Tangut fortress name
lofty / phonetic element in Tangut fortress name

b_shengwei.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription of a Tangut fortress name (Shengweicheng / 省嵬城), built in 1024 CE on the northern approach to the Yinchuan Plain.

b_zhongcun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; generic Chinese settlement name ('Middle Village') with no documented pre-867 CE historical attestation in the Keyimen / Helan Mountain region.

b_wuliji.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; modern Mongolian-named administrative unit (Wuliji Sumu / 乌力吉苏木) in Alxa Left Banner, Inner Mongolia.
b_wuliji.etymology_analysis: Sinicization of Mongolian ölzii / üljii ('auspicious, fortunate'). The repo calque ('Raven + Strength + Propitious') misinterprets the Chinese phonetic characters 乌力吉 literally.

b_wuluhai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1209 CE during Genghis Khan's campaign against Western Xia, when Mongol forces captured Wuluhai City (兀剌海城 / Uraqai), seat of the Heishan Weifu Military Command.

morphemes.translation: transliteration of the Western Xia / Yuan fortress name Uraqai

b_wuluhai.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription of Uraqai (兀剌海), a Western Xia fortress near a pass in the Langshan (Yinshan) Mountains, later Yuan Wuluhai Route.

b_dengkou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dengkou County (磴口县) in January 1929 CE under Ningxia Province (named after a Yellow River cliff-step landing).
b_dengkou.etymology_analysis: Chinese compound meaning 'Stone-Step Crossing' (磴口), referring to a Yellow River landing/ferry point in western Inner Mongolia.

historical_names.name: Shuofang Commandery
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu): Han Emperor Wu established Shuofang Commandery in 127 BCE in the territory of modern Dengkou County.
historical_names.notes: Modern Dengkou County encompasses the Western Han Shuofang Commandery seat (127 BCE), though the name Dengkou dates to 1929 CE.

b_helan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for a settlement/county named Helan; Helan County was established in 1941 CE (named after the Helan Mountains, attested from the Sui dynasty c. 581 CE).

morphemes.translation: piebald horse (ethnonym of the Helan tribe)

b_helan.etymology_analysis: Sinicization of the tribal name Helan (explained in Tang Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi as 'piebald horse' in northern nomadic speech), applied to the Helan Mountains by the Sui dynasty. Modern Helan County dates to 1941 CE.

historical_names.name: Beiyi Shan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise, compiled 111 CE): 'Lian County, Beiyi Mountain is to the northwest.'
historical_names.notes: Known as Beiyi Mountain (卑移山) in the Han dynasty before being renamed Helan Mountain by the Sui dynasty.

b_huaiyuan.first_mention_attestation: Northern Zhou Emperor Wu established Huaiyuan Commandery and Huaiyuan County (怀远县) in Jiande 3rd year (574 CE) at Yinhan City (modern Yinchuan, Ningxia).
b_huaiyuan.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Cherish the Distant Frontier' (怀远), established by Northern Zhou in 574 CE and maintained as a Tang county and town.

historical_names.name: Yinhan City
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (813 CE): 'Originally named Yinhan City; Helian Bobo made it Lizi Garden (407–431 CE).'
historical_names.notes: Originally Yinhan City (饮汗城) under Sixteen Kingdoms Xia before Northern Zhou established Huaiyuan County in 574 CE.

b_dingyaun.first_mention_attestation: Tang Emperor Xuanzong Xiantian 1st year (712 CE): Shuofang Grand Commander Guo Yuanzhen built Dingyuan Military City (定远军城) near Yaofu Town, Pingluo County, Ningxia.
b_dingyaun.etymology_analysis: Chinese military-administrative name meaning 'Pacify the Distant Frontier' (定远; barony_key 'b_dingyaun' is a romanization typo for Dingyuan), founded in 712 CE.

b_baojing.first_mention_attestation: Tang Zhide 1st year (756 CE): Anjing County under Lingzhou was renamed Baojing County (保静县), located near Wanghong in Yongning County, Ningxia.
b_baojing.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Preserve Tranquility' (保静), renamed from Anjing County in 756 CE.

historical_names.name: Anjing County
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang: Anjing County under Lingzhou prior to being renamed Baojing in 756 CE.
historical_names.notes: Previously called Anjing County (安静县) before 756 CE.

b_linhe.first_mention_attestation: Western Wei (535–557 CE) established Linhe Commandery (临河郡), seated at Linhe County (临河县) under Lingzhou in the northern Ningxia Plain.
b_linhe.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Overlooking the River' (临河), referring to its position along the Yellow River in Lingzhou.

b_huining.first_mention_attestation: Western Wei Feidi 2nd year (553 CE) established Huizhou and Huining County (会宁县) in modern Jingyuan/Huining, Gansu.
b_huining.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Assembly of Peace' (会宁), derived from Western Wei Huizhou ('Assembly Prefecture', 553 CE).

historical_names.name: Zuli
historical_names.source: Shiji / Book of Han: Western Han established Zuli and Chunyin counties in 114 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Western Wei Huining County (553 CE) was established on former Western Han Chunyin / Zuli territory.

historical_names.name: Chunyin
