historical_names.source: Shiji / Book of Han: Western Han established Zuli and Chunyin counties in 114 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Western Wei Huining County (553 CE) was established on former Western Han Chunyin / Zuli territory.

b_huairong_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Song dynasty biography of Guo Cheng (1047–1102 CE), who was ordered during the late 11th/early 12th century (c. 1099–1102 CE) to build Suirong and Huairong forts (怀戎堡) on the Song–Western Xia frontier.
b_huairong_2.etymology_analysis: Chinese frontier fort name meaning 'Conciliate the Western Peoples' (怀戎), built during the Song–Western Xia border wars.

b_tiandu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Northern Song Xianping 5th year (1002 CE), when Tangut forces occupied Tiandu Mountain (天都山) in modern Haiyuan County, Ningxia; later seat of Western Xia Left Flank Shenyong Military Command.
b_tiandu.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym meaning 'Heavenly Metropolis' (天都山), prominent in Western Xia military and palace history in Haiyuan County, Ningxia.

b_huichuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Jin dynasty (post-1183 CE), when Jin established an emigrant Huizhou ('New Huizhou') at Huichuan City (会川城, southwest of modern Jingyuan County, Gansu) after Western Xia retook old Huizhou.
b_huichuan.etymology_analysis: Chinese settlement name meaning 'Converging River Valley' (会川), attested as Huichuan City in the Jin dynasty.

b_huile.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the start of the Sui dynasty (Kaihuang 1st year, 581 CE) as Huile County (回乐县), the seat of Lingzhou in modern Litong District, Wuzhong, Ningxia.
b_huile.etymology_analysis: Chinese county name meaning 'Return to Joy/Peace' (回乐), established by the Sui dynasty as the seat of Lingzhou. The repo calque anachronistically links 回 to the later Uyghur ethnonym Huihe.

historical_names.name: Bogulu Town
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Zhangjiashan Han slips: Han Emperor Hui 4th year (191 BCE) established Lingzhou County; Northern Wei later established Bogulu Town.
historical_names.notes: Huile County (581 CE) served as the seat of Lingzhou (Wuzhong), succeeding Northern Wei Bogulu Town and Han Lingzhou.

historical_names.name: Lingzhou
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) / Zhangjiashan Han slips: Han Emperor Hui 4th year (191 BCE) established Lingzhou County; Northern Wei later established Bogulu Town.
historical_names.notes: Huile County (581 CE) served as the seat of Lingzhou (Wuzhong), succeeding Northern Wei Bogulu Town and Han Lingzhou.

b_lingwu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE census) as Lingwu County (灵武县) under Beidi Commandery; later Sui Daye 3rd year (607 CE) Lingwu Commandery.
b_lingwu.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Numinous Martiality' (灵武), attested since Western Han Beidi Commandery.

b_yaode.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Songshi Jishi Benmo (juan 14, Xianping era c. 999–1002 CE) in proposals to build Pule and Yaode cities (耀德城) to secure grain supply routes to Lingwu against Li Jiqian.
b_yaode.etymology_analysis: Chinese fortress name meaning 'Glorify Virtue' (耀德), proposed/built during the Northern Song defense of Lingzhou.

b_anle.first_mention_attestation: Tang Emperor Gaozong Xianheng 3rd year (672 CE) split Mingsha County of Lingzhou to establish Anle Prefecture (安乐州), seated at Anle City (modern Hongchengshui, Weizhou, Tongxin County, Ningxia), to settle Tuyuhun Murong tribes.
b_anle.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Peace and Joy' (安乐), established by Tang in 672 CE for resettled Tuyuhun tribes.

b_wenchi_2.first_mention_attestation: Tang Shenlong era (705–709 CE; Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi notes Shenlong 5th year / 709 CE, local gazetteers 705/706 CE) established Wenchi County (温池县) near a salt pond in modern Yanchi County, Ningxia.
b_wenchi_2.etymology_analysis: Chinese county name meaning 'Warm Pool' (温池), named after a local salt pond in Tang Lingzhou/Weizhou.

b_changhua.first_mention_attestation: Later Jin Tianfu 7th year (942 CE) abolished Xiongzhou and renamed it Changhua Military Prefecture (昌化军) under Lingzhou; in Northern Song it became Changhua Town (昌化镇) in modern Zhongwei, Ningxia.
b_changhua.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name meaning 'Prosperous Transformation' (昌化), instituted in 942 CE.

historical_names.name: Xiongzhou
historical_names.source: Tang Xuanzong Dazhong 3rd year (849 CE) established Xiongzhou; abolished in 942 CE to become Changhua Military Prefecture.
historical_names.notes: Changhua Military Prefecture (942 CE) succeeded Tang Xiongzhou (849 CE) in the Zhongwei/Zhongning region.

historical_names.name: Chengtianbao
historical_names.source: Tang Xuanzong Dazhong 3rd year (849 CE) established Xiongzhou; abolished in 942 CE to become Changhua Military Prefecture.
historical_names.notes: Changhua Military Prefecture (942 CE) succeeded Tang Xiongzhou (849 CE) in the Zhongwei/Zhongning region.

b_wulan.first_mention_attestation: Northern Zhou Baoding 3rd year (563 CE): Emperor Wu toured west and established Wulan Pass (乌兰关) and Wulan County (乌兰县) in modern Jingyuan County, Gansu (also attested in Sui/Tang tomb epitaphs from Beichengtan).

morphemes.translation: dark, black (or phonetic element in Wulan)

b_wulan.etymology_analysis: Northern Zhou pass and county name (乌兰, likely transcribing a northern/steppe word for 'red' or 'pass'), attested from 563 CE in Jingyuan, Gansu.

historical_names.name: Zuli County
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi / Book of Han: Western Han established Zuli County in 114 BCE on the territory later occupied by Wulan County.
historical_names.notes: Northern Zhou Wulan County (563 CE) was established on former Western Han Zuli County territory.

b_roulang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 11th-century Western Xia and Song records as Roulang Mountain (柔狼山) in modern Pingchuan/Jingyuan, Gansu, where the Western Xia Xishou Baotai Military Command was stationed.
b_roulang.etymology_analysis: Oronym Roulang Mountain (柔狼山), attested in Song–Western Xia frontier geography.

b_shatuo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tang dynasty histories (Old Book of Tang, New Book of Tang, Zizhi Tongjian) from the 7th century CE for the Shatuo (沙陀) Turkic tribe, and specifically in 809 CE when the Shatuo under Zhuye Jinzhong and Zhuye Zhiyi arrived at Lingzhou and were settled in Yanzhou (Yanchi, Ningxia).
b_shatuo.etymology_analysis: Chinese ethnonym/toponym Shatuo (沙陀), meaning 'Sand Dunes', originally denoting the desert habitat (Shatuo Qi) of the Chuyue Turkic tribe who were resettled in Lingzhou/Yanzhou in 809 CE.

b_mingsha.first_mention_attestation: Northern Zhou Jiande 6th year (577 CE): abolished commandery and established Mingsha Town (鸣沙镇); Sui Kaihuang 19th year (599 CE) established Mingsha County (鸣沙县) in modern Zhongning County, Ningxia.
b_mingsha.etymology_analysis: Chinese settlement name meaning 'Singing Sands' (鸣沙), derived from the acoustic sand dunes along the Yellow River in Zhongning County.

historical_names.name: Fuping County
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi / Shiji: Qin-Han Fuping County; Northern Zhou Baoding 2nd year (562 CE) moved Huizhou here.
historical_names.notes: Prior to Mingsha Town (577 CE), the area was Qin-Han Fuping County and the relocated seat of Huizhou (562 CE).

historical_names.name: Huizhou
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi / Shiji: Qin-Han Fuping County; Northern Zhou Baoding 2nd year (562 CE) moved Huizhou here.
historical_names.notes: Prior to Mingsha Town (577 CE), the area was Qin-Han Fuping County and the relocated seat of Huizhou (562 CE).

b_fengan.first_mention_attestation: Sui Daye 3rd year (607 CE) Fengan County (丰安县) under Lingwu Commandery; later Tang Wansui Tongtian 1st year (696 CE) Fengan Military Command (丰安军) at Shikong Town, Zhongning County, Ningxia.
b_fengan.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative and military name meaning 'Abundant Peace' (丰安), attested from 607 CE.

b_xiashi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; no contemporary written or epigraphic attestation <= 867 CE exists for a settlement named 'Xiashi' (峡石) in the Xiongzhou / Zhongwei region of Ningxia.

b_weijing.first_mention_attestation: Attested in History of Song (Songshi, juan 485, Xia Guo Zhuan) for the 11th-century Western Xia military deployment at Weijing Mountain (惟精山) guarding the southern frontier toward Huan, Qing, Zhenyuan, and Yuan prefectures.
b_weijing.etymology_analysis: Chinese oronym Weijing Mountain (惟精山), attested in 11th-century Song–Western Xia frontier records.

b_jiuyuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 300 BCE (26th year of King Wuling of Zhao) in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) as the western frontier region of Jiuyuan (九原), later established as Jiuyuan Commandery under the Qin dynasty in 214 BCE.
b_jiuyuan.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym 九原 (Jiǔyuán, 'Nine Plains'), referring to the nine flat alluvial terraces/plateaus along the northern Ordos bend of the Yellow River near modern Baotou.

b_yongfeng.first_mention_attestation: Established in 650 CE (23rd year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Yongfeng County (永丰县) under Fengzhou Prefecture, recorded in the Xin Tangshu (New Book of Tang).
b_yongfeng.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese administrative name 永丰 (Yǒngfēng, 'Perpetual Abundance'), bestowed when the Tang dynasty re-established Fengzhou in the Hetao region.

b_xishouxiang.first_mention_attestation: Constructed in 708 CE (2nd year of Jinglong, Tang dynasty) by general Zhang Renyuan as the Western Surrender-Receiving City (西受降城), one of the Three Surrender-Receiving Cities along the northern Yellow River.
b_xishouxiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese military fortress name 西受降城 (Xī Shòuxiángchéng, 'Western Surrender-Receiving Fortress'), built to receive submissions from Turkic tribes and anchor the Tang northern frontier.

b_tiande.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tiande Jun (天德军) in 758 CE (1st year of Qianyuan, Tang dynasty) from Da'an Jun (大安军), which had been founded in 753–755 CE in the Hetao plain.
b_tiande.etymology_analysis: Chinese military garrison name 天德军 (Tiāndéjūn, 'Heavenly Virtue Army'), an auspicious imperial title for the Tang frontier command in northern Hetao.

historical_names.name: Da'an Jun
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi & Xin Tangshu (built 753–755 CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally built as Da'an Jun (大安军) in 753–755 CE before being renamed Tiande Jun in 758 CE.

historical_names.name: Tian'an Jun
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi & Xin Tangshu (built 753–755 CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally built as Da'an Jun (大安军) in 753–755 CE before being renamed Tiande Jun in 758 CE.

b_zhongshouxiang.first_mention_attestation: Constructed in 708 CE (2nd year of Jinglong, Tang dynasty) by general Zhang Renyuan as the Central Surrender-Receiving City (中受降城), near modern Baotou.
b_zhongshouxiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese military fortress name 中受降城 (Zhōng Shòuxiángchéng, 'Central Surrender-Receiving Fortress'), the central bastion of Zhang Renyuan's Three Surrender-Receiving Cities.

b_quye.first_mention_attestation: First prominently attested in 1057 CE (2nd year of Jiayou, Northern Song) in the Songshi (History of Song, vol. 485) as the Quye River (屈野河) borderland contested between Northern Song and Western Xia.
b_quye.etymology_analysis: Hydronym 屈野河 (Qūyě Hé, today Kuye River 窟野河), a tributary of the Yellow River in northern Shaanxi; no pre-867 CE written attestation of a settlement or river named Quye is recorded.

b_dijin.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 982 CE (7th year of Taiping Xingguo, Northern Song) in the Songshi (vol. 485) as Dijin Marsh (地斤泽), the desert oasis northeast of Xiazhou to which Tangut leader Li Jiqian fled.
b_dijin.etymology_analysis: Toponym 地斤泽 (Dìjīnzé), a desert oasis/marsh in the Ordos (modern Otog Banner); the Chinese characters likely transcribe an earlier non-Han/Tangut or nomadic place name rather than literally meaning 'land + axe'.

b_huanshui.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE or standard historical gazetteers for the Quye/northern Shaanxi region; the repo's b_origin cites 明堂 ('Bright Hall') rather than Huanshui.
b_huanshui.etymology_analysis: Barony key b_huanshui (Huanshui) has no confirmed historical settlement attestation in the Quye/Xiasui region, and the existing repo metadata mismatches it with 明堂 (Míngtáng, 'Bright Hall').

b_longquan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Longquan County (龙泉县) in 742 CE (1st year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) from Shangxian (上县), serving as the seat of Suizhou (modern Suide County, Shaanxi).
b_longquan.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym 龙泉 (Lóngquán, 'Dragon Spring'), named after a local spring in Suide during the Tang Tianbao renaming.

historical_names.name: Shangxian
historical_names.source: Suishu & Xin Tangshu (established under Western Wei)
historical_names.notes: Originally established as Shangxian (上县) under Western Wei before being renamed Longquan County in 742 CE.

b_suide.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 543 CE (9th year of Datong, Western Wei), when Lu Tong was enfeoffed as Duke of Suide Commandery (绥德郡), with Suide County as its seat.
b_suide.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 绥德 (Suídé, 'Pacify through Virtue'), reflecting Northern Dynasties frontier governance in northern Shaanxi.

b_yanfu.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 605 CE (1st year of Daye, Sui dynasty) under Shangzhou/Diaoyin Commandery as Yanfu County (延福县), renamed during the Sui Kaihuang–Daye eras from Western Wei Yanling County.
b_yanfu.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chinese county name 延福 (Yánfú, 'Prolonged Blessing'), replacing the earlier Western Wei name Yanling.

historical_names.name: Yanling County
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyuji vol. 38 (established 1st year of Feidi, Western Wei)
historical_names.notes: Established as Yanling County (延陵县) in 552 CE under Western Wei and renamed Yanfu County under Sui.

b_wuyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 127 BCE (2nd year of Yuanshuo, Western Han) when Wei Qing recovered the Hetao region and Emperor Wu founded Wuyuan Commandery (五原郡), recorded in the Hanshu.
b_wuyuan.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym 五原 (Wǔyuán, 'Five Plains'), referring to the five elevated plains in the Hetao/Yanzhou region.

b_baichi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Baichi County (白池县) in 708 CE (2nd year of Jinglong, Tang dynasty) from Xingning County, named after the white salt lake (白池) in Yanzhou (Taiping Huanyuji, vol. 37).
b_baichi.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym 白池 (Báichí, 'White Pool'), named after the white-encrusted salt lake in Yanzhou.

historical_names.name: Xingning County
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyuji vol. 37 (Tang Wude 1st year / Zhenguan 2nd year)
historical_names.notes: Previously Xingning County (兴宁县) before being renamed Baichi County in 708 CE.

b_hengshan_3.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1041 CE (1st year of Qingli, Northern Song) in the Xu Zizhi Tongjian Changbian (vol. 132) as the strategic Hengshan (横山) mountain range dividing Song and Western Xia.
b_hengshan_3.etymology_analysis: Oronym 横山 (Héngshān, 'Transverse Mountain'), describing the east-west loess ridge between the Mu Us Desert and Loess Plateau; Hengshan County itself was only named in 1914 CE.

b_pule.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested in 1002 CE (Northern Song Xianping 5th year) in Songshi Jishi Benmo (Vol. 14), recording official He Liang's (何亮) memorial proposing to build Pule (溥樂) and Yaode (耀德) cities ('請築溥樂、耀德二城') to secure grain supply routes to Lingwu against Li Jiqian.
b_pule.etymology_analysis: Chinese auspicious fortress compound 溥樂 (Pǔlè, 'Vast Joy'), attested in 1002 CE in Northern Song official He Liang's memorial proposing to build Pule and Yaode cities along the Lingwu supply route.

b_shuofang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 127 BCE (2nd year of Yuanshuo, Western Han) as Shuofang Commandery and County (朔方郡/朔方县) after Wei Qing's campaign, recorded in the Hanshu.
b_shuofang.etymology_analysis: Classical Chinese directional-regional name 朔方 (Shuòfāng, 'Northern Region'), used in the Book of Documents and adopted by Han Emperor Wu for the Ordos commandery.

b_ningshuo.first_mention_attestation: Established under the Northern Zhou (557–581 CE) as Ningshuo County (宁朔县) under Huazheng Commandery, later subordinate to Xiazhou in the Sui and Tang dynasties (Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi).
b_ningshuo.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 宁朔 (Níngshuò, 'Pacify the North'), a frontier county in Xiazhou.

b_dejing.first_mention_attestation: Elevated to Dejing County (德静县) in 613 CE (9th year of Daye, Sui dynasty) from Dejing Garrison, recorded in the Xin Tangshu (vol. 37) under Xiazhou.
b_dejing.etymology_analysis: Chinese frontier garrison and county name 德静 (Déjìng, 'Virtuous Tranquility'), located southwest of Tongwancheng in Xiazhou.

historical_names.name: Mihun Garrison
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyuji / Xin Tangshu (established under Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou)
historical_names.notes: Originally Mihun Garrison (弥浑戍) under Northern Zhou before Sui renamed it Dejing Garrison and then Dejing County in 613 CE.

b_wuyan.first_mention_attestation: Constructed in 824 CE (4th year of Changqing, Tang dynasty) as Wuyan Fortress (乌延城) in Jingbian, later rebuilt as Zhenjingbao during the Ming dynasty.
b_wuyan.etymology_analysis: Tang frontier fortress name 乌延城 (Wūyánchéng), likely echoing the local Wushui/Sheyan (乌水/奢延) hydronyms of the Xiazhou borderland.

b_rulin.first_mention_attestation: Established in 583 CE (3rd year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) as Rulin County (儒林县), serving as the seat of Yinzhou (银州) in northern Shaanxi.
b_rulin.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 儒林 (Rúlín, 'Forest of Scholars'), the seat of Yinzhou from the Sui through Tang dynasties.

b_zhenxiang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 581 CE (1st year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) as Zhenxiang County (真乡县) under Zhenxiang Commandery in Yinzhou.
b_zhenxiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 真乡 (Zhēnxiāng, 'True Township'), a county under Yinzhou in the Sui and Tang dynasties.

b_kaiguang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 562 CE (2nd year of Baoding, Northern Zhou) as Kaiguang County (开光县) and seat of Kaiguang Commandery, later part of Yinzhou.
b_kaiguang.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 开光 (Kāiguāng, 'Opening Light'), founded by Northern Zhou in northeastern Yulin/Jia County.

b_changze.first_mention_attestation: Established under the Northern Wei (by 534 CE) as Changze County (长泽县) under Da'an Commandery in Changzhou (Inner Mongolia/Ordos), later transferred to Xiazhou and Youzhou.
b_changze.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym 长泽 (Chángzé, 'Long Marsh'), referring to a marshland in the southern Ordos; seat of New Youzhou from 820 CE.

b_yanen.first_mention_attestation: Established in 679 CE (1st year of Tiaolu, Tang dynasty) as Yan'en County (延恩县), seat of Yizhou (one of the Six Hu Prefectures) and later of Youzhou in 738 CE.
b_yanen.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 延恩 (Yán'ēn, 'Prolonged Imperial Grace'), reflecting Tang pacification and resettlement of Sogdian/Turkic groups in the Ordos.

b_guiren_2.first_mention_attestation: Established in 738 CE (26th year of Kaiyuan, Tang dynasty) as Guiren County (归仁县) under Youzhou, renamed from Changquan County of Lanchi Prefecture.
b_guiren_2.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 归仁 (Guīrén, 'Returning to Benevolence'), bestowed upon the submitted Sogdian/Turkic settlement in Youzhou.

historical_names.name: Changquan County
historical_names.source: Wikipedia (归仁县) & Tang administrative records (Lanchi Prefecture, 709 CE)
historical_names.notes: Formerly Changquan County (长泉县) under Lanchi Prefecture before being renamed Guiren County in 738 CE.

b_huaide_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 757 CE (2nd year of Zhide, Tang dynasty) as Huaide County (怀德县) under Huaide Commandery / Youzhou in the Ordos (modern Otog Front Banner).
b_huaide_2.etymology_analysis: Chinese administrative name 怀德 (Huáidé, 'Cherishing Virtue'), a Tang county in Youzhou.

b_alxa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Qing records in 1689 CE (28th year of Kangxi) as the pastureland of Alashan/Alxa (阿拉善), where the Khoshut Mongols were settled and organized into the Alxa Banner in 1697 CE.

natural_proper_name.name: Alxa / Helan Mountains (阿拉善/贺兰山)

morphemes.translation: pied horse / variegated (from the Helan Mountains)

b_alxa.etymology_analysis: Mongolic toponym Alxa (阿拉善, also transcribed 阿剌筛), derived from the Mongolic name of the Helan Mountains (meaning 'pied/dappled horse').

b_yabulai.first_mention_attestation: Modern Inner Mongolian town (Yabulai Town, 雅布赖镇) and salt lake (Yabarai Davsan Nuur) in Alxa Right Banner; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_yabulai.etymology_analysis: Chinese phonetic transcription 雅布赖 (Yǎbùlài) of Mongolic Yabarai; the repo's character-by-character calque ('classical elegance + linen + rely') is a folk/literal misreading of a Mongolic transcription.

b_tamusubulage.first_mention_attestation: Modern sumu (Tamusubulage Sumu, 塔木素布拉格苏木) in Alxa Right Banner, Inner Mongolia; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_tamusubulage.etymology_analysis: Chinese phonetic transcription 塔木素布拉格 of Mongolic Tamsagbulag ('Sweet Spring'); the repo's calque ('pagoda + wood + linen...') is a literal misreading of the transcription characters.

b_chaganbulage.first_mention_attestation: Modern gacha and salt lake (Chaganbulage Salt Lake, 查干布拉格盐池) in Alxa Left Banner, Inner Mongolia; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

natural_proper_name.name: Chaganbulage Salt Lake (查干布拉格盐池)

b_chaganbulage.etymology_analysis: Chinese phonetic transcription 查干布拉格 of Mongolic Čagan Bulag ('White Spring'), named after the white salt spring/lake.

b_chaogetuhure.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Qing-era Tibetan Buddhist records in 1716 CE (55th year of Kangxi), when the 6th Dalai Lama visited the site of Chaogetu Hure (朝格图呼热, later Zhaohua Temple) in Alxa Left Banner.
b_chaogetuhure.etymology_analysis: Chinese phonetic transcription 超格图呼热 of Mongolic Čogtu Küriy-e ('Glorious Monastery', Zhaohua Temple), founded in the early Qing dynasty.

b_zhenfan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1397 CE (30th year of Hongwu, Ming dynasty) as Zhenfan Guard (镇番卫), later renamed Zhenfan County in 1724 CE and Minqin County in 1928 CE.
b_zhenfan.etymology_analysis: Ming military guard name 镇番卫 (Zhènfān Wèi, 'Guard Against the Frontier Tribes'), founded in 1397 CE in the Hexi-Tengger corridor.

b_jiahe.first_mention_attestation: Modern town (Jiahe Town, 夹河镇) in Minqin County, Gansu; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_jiahe.etymology_analysis: Chinese toponym 夹河 (Jiāhé, 'Between the Rivers'), a modern township in Minqin County.
